tool.name: AspectFocalStatistics
tool.summary: Neighborhood (focal) statistics for an aspect raster, computed with circular statistics. Aspect is a circular variable -- 0 and 360 degrees are the same direction -- so ordinary Focal Statistics, which treats it as a plain number, is wrong. This tool offers circular measures of central tendency and dispersion (mean direction, circular variance, standard deviation, resultant length, range, Rayleigh test, von Mises concentration, and more) over any neighborhood shape, on projected or geographic aspect rasters, and needs no Spatial Analyst.
tool.usage:
Why aspect matters. Aspect -- the compass direction a slope faces -- has a long history in habitat and vegetation analysis because different aspects carry different vegetation and microclimate: north- and south-facing slopes (in the northern hemisphere) differ markedly in temperature, moisture, and the communities they support. The underlying driver is solar energy: the amount of direct sunlight a slope receives is what actually shapes those differences. For that reason solar insolation -- a function of aspect together with slope, shading from surrounding topography, atmospheric conditions, and surface reflectivity -- often captures what makes aspect ecologically important better than aspect alone. Where the amount of received sunlight is the real variable of interest, consider estimating insolation directly (for example with Esri's Solar Radiation tool) rather than using aspect as a surrogate. Aspect remains valuable because it is simple, fast, and a good predictor in many settings. (These points, and the circular-statistics methods below, follow Jenness, J. 2012, "Directions: making sense of directional data.")
Why circular statistics. Aspect is a circular (directional) variable: 359 degrees and 1 degree are two degrees apart, not 358, and the ordinary arithmetic mean of 359 and 1 is 180 (due south) -- the exact opposite of the correct answer (due north). Every statistic here is computed by the correct circular method: each aspect is treated as a unit vector, the vectors are summed, and the length and direction of that resultant drive all the measures. This tool mirrors Esri's Focal Statistics -- the same neighborhood shapes -- but produces circular statistics and requires no Spatial Analyst. It is intended only for aspect (and other true circular rasters such as D-infinity flow direction), not for ordinary continuous rasters.
Statistics (one per run):
• Central tendency: Mean Direction (the circular mean, in compass degrees) and Median Direction (the circular median -- a more robust center). • Dispersion: Circular Variance (0 = all cells face the same way, 1 = maximally dispersed or balanced), Angular Variance, Circular Standard Deviation and Angular Deviation (both in degrees), and Circular Range (the smallest arc, in degrees, containing all the aspects). • Concentration: Mean Resultant Length (0 to 1; near 1 means tightly clustered directions) and the von Mises Concentration kappa (0 = uniform, larger = more concentrated). • Testing: the Rayleigh Test p-value (small p = a statistically preferred direction; large p = no preferred direction). • Proportion With Defined Aspect: the fraction of the neighborhood that is not flat.
Flat cells. An aspect of -1 means a flat cell with no direction. Flat cells carry no aspect, so they are ignored in every neighborhood. When a neighborhood contains a mix of flat and sloped cells, only the sloped cells contribute. When every cell in a neighborhood is flat, the result depends on the statistic: Mean Direction and Median Direction are set to -1 (the flat sentinel); Circular Variance, Angular Variance, Circular Standard Deviation, Angular Deviation, and Circular Range are set to 0 (no directional variation); Mean Resultant Length and the Rayleigh p-value are set to 1; von Mises kappa is set to -1; and Proportion With Defined Aspect is 0. Alternatively, set "All-flat neighborhoods" to NoData to leave those cells out of the result entirely (useful when flat areas should be excluded from later analysis). Cells that have no valid neighbor at all (outside the data, or entirely NoData) are always NoData.
Neighborhoods and units. All Focal-Statistics neighborhood shapes are available: Rectangle (width x height), Circle (radius), Annulus (inner and outer radius), Wedge (radius plus start and end angles, measured counter-clockwise from east), and Irregular / Weight from an ASCII kernel file (first line "ncols nrows", then the matrix; Irregular = 0/1, Weight = weights). Sizes are given in Cells or in a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles). On a projected raster the neighborhood is a fixed number of cells; on a geographic (latitude/longitude) raster, where cell size in ground units changes with latitude, a ground-unit neighborhood is sized geodesically per row -- the same treatment the other tools in this toolbox use. Kernel-file neighborhoods are defined directly in cells.
D-infinity flow direction. The D-infinity (DINF) flow-direction algorithm reports the direction of steepest descent -- which is essentially aspect -- but in the mathematical convention (0 = east, increasing counter-clockwise), not the compass convention of an ordinary aspect raster (0 = north, increasing clockwise). All the dispersion, concentration, and testing statistics are identical either way (they are unaffected by where 0 sits or which way angles turn); only Mean Direction and Median Direction depend on the convention. Set "Input aspect convention" to Mathematical when the input is a DINF raster, and the tool converts those direction outputs to compass so they match an ordinary aspect analysis. If the tool detects a DINF raster from its geoprocessing history it suggests this setting automatically and warns if it is left on Compass. (A standard D8 flow-direction raster stores flow codes 1-128, not degrees, and is not valid input.)
Direction outputs are always reported in compass degrees; flat neighborhoods are -1 (or NoData). Mean Direction and Median Direction outputs are symbolized with a cyclic aspect color scheme (bluegreen - yellow - brown - yellow - bluegreen, so 0 and 360 degrees share the same color), with flat (-1) drawn separately in a mask color; the other statistics get a blue-to-red stretch. This tool honors no geoprocessing environments. References: circular statistics follow Mardia and Jupp (2000), Fisher (1993), Batschelet (1981), and Zar (1999); the von Mises concentration estimate follows Fisher (1993) / Best and Fisher (1981); see also Jenness (2012).

dialogReference.para: A single-band aspect raster in degrees, 0-360 measured clockwise from north (compass), with -1 for flat cells. A D-infinity flow-direction raster is also valid input -- set the Input aspect convention to Mathematical for it (see below).
The output raster for the chosen statistic. A name is suggested from the input and the statistic. A folder path typed without an extension is written as a GeoTIFF.
The circular statistic to compute (one per run):

bulletList.bullet_item: Circular Variance, Angular Variance, Circular Standard Deviation, Angular Deviation, Circular Range (dispersion)
Mean Resultant Length, von Mises Concentration (kappa) (concentration)

dialogReference.para: See the tool description for definitions and for the value used where a whole neighborhood is flat.
The neighborhood shape: Rectangle, Circle, Annulus, Wedge, or Irregular / Weight (from a kernel file). The relevant size parameters below become active for the chosen shape.

The units for the neighborhood size: Cells, or a ground unit (Meters, Kilometers, Feet, Miles). On a geographic raster a ground unit is sized geodesically per row. Not used for kernel-file neighborhoods, which are defined in cells.
The neighborhood radius (Circle and Wedge), in the chosen units.
The rectangle width, in the chosen units (Rectangle neighborhood).
The rectangle height, in the chosen units (Rectangle neighborhood).
The inner radius of the ring (Annulus neighborhood), in the chosen units. Cells inside this radius are excluded.
The outer radius of the ring (Annulus neighborhood), in the chosen units. Must be greater than the Inner radius.
The wedge's starting angle in degrees, measured counter-clockwise from east (Wedge neighborhood). The wedge spans counter-clockwise from the start angle to the End angle.
The wedge's ending angle in degrees, measured counter-clockwise from east (Wedge neighborhood).

An ASCII kernel file for the Irregular or Weight neighborhood: the first line is "ncols nrows", followed by the matrix. Irregular files use 0 (excluded) and 1 (included); Weight files hold weights (0 = excluded). The kernel is centered on each cell and defined in cells.

The angular convention of the input. Choose Compass for an ordinary aspect raster (0 = north, increasing clockwise). Choose Mathematical for a D-infinity (DINF) flow-direction raster: DINF reports the direction of steepest descent -- essentially aspect -- but in the mathematical convention (0 = east, increasing counter-clockwise), which most users do not realize. With Mathematical selected, the tool reads the angles correctly and converts the Mean Direction and Median Direction outputs to compass. All other statistics are the same under either convention. The tool suggests this setting automatically when it detects a DINF raster.

What to write where every cell in a neighborhood is flat (aspect -1, no direction). Sentinel uses a per-statistic value (-1 for direction, 0 for dispersion, 1 for resultant length and Rayleigh p, -1 for kappa, 0 for proportion). NoData leaves those cells out of the result entirely.

scriptExample.title: Aspect Focal Statistics example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Circular mean aspect over a 3-cell circle, then circular variance over a 5x5 rectangle, then a D-infinity raster read in the mathematical convention. Valid statistic values are exactly: "Mean Direction", "Median Direction", "Mean Resultant Length", "Circular Variance", "Angular Variance", "Circular Standard Deviation", "Angular Deviation", "Circular Range", "Rayleigh Test p-value", "von Mises Concentration (kappa)", "Proportion With Defined Aspect". neighborhood: "Rectangle", "Circle", "Annulus", "Wedge", "Irregular", "Weight". nbr_units: "Cells", "Meters", "Kilometers", "Feet", "Miles". input_convention: "Compass (0 = north, clockwise)", "Mathematical (0 = east, counter-clockwise; e.g. D-infinity)". flat_handling: "Sentinel (-1 / 0 / 1 by statistic)", "NoData". Unused neighborhood arguments may be left as-is; only the ones for the chosen shape are read.
scriptExample.code:
import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your installed path is shown in this tool's run messages
# Circular mean aspect over a 3-cell-radius circle arcpy.jenness.AspectFocalStatistics( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\aspect", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\aspect_MeanDir", statistic="Mean Direction", neighborhood="Circle", nbr_units="Cells", radius=3, input_convention="Compass (0 = north, clockwise)", flat_handling="Sentinel (-1 / 0 / 1 by statistic)")
# Circular variance over a 5 x 5 rectangle arcpy.jenness.AspectFocalStatistics( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\aspect", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\aspect_CVar", statistic="Circular Variance", neighborhood="Rectangle", nbr_units="Cells", width=5, height=5)
# A D-infinity flow-direction raster (mathematical convention); Mean Direction # is converted to compass in the output. arcpy.jenness.AspectFocalStatistics( in_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\flowdir_dinf", out_raster=r"C:\Project\Terrain.gdb\dinf_MeanDir", statistic="Mean Direction", neighborhood="Circle", nbr_units="Cells", radius=3, input_convention="Mathematical (0 = east, counter-clockwise; e.g. D-infinity)")

dataIdInfo.idPurp: Neighborhood (focal) statistics for an aspect raster using circular statistics -- mean direction, circular variance/standard deviation, resultant length, range, Rayleigh test, von Mises concentration, and more -- over any neighborhood shape, projected or geographic, with no Spatial Analyst.
dataIdInfo.idAbs: Aspect is a circular variable (0 and 360 degrees are the same direction), so ordinary Focal Statistics gives wrong answers. This tool computes circular statistics over a neighborhood of each cell: Mean Direction, Median Direction, Mean Resultant Length, Circular Variance, Angular Variance, Circular Standard Deviation, Angular Deviation, Circular Range, Rayleigh Test p-value, von Mises Concentration (kappa), and Proportion With Defined Aspect. All Focal-Statistics neighborhood shapes are supported (Rectangle, Circle, Annulus, Wedge, Irregular, Weight), in cells or ground units, with geodesic per-row sizing on geographic rasters and no Spatial Analyst requirement. Flat cells (aspect -1) are ignored; the all-flat fill is per-statistic (or NoData). D-infinity flow-direction rasters -- essentially aspect in the mathematical convention (0 = east, counter-clockwise) -- are supported via a convention toggle that converts the direction outputs to compass. Aspect matters ecologically because different aspects carry different vegetation and microclimate, driven by received solar energy; where that energy is the variable of interest, solar insolation may capture it better than aspect alone. Circular statistics follow Mardia and Jupp (2000), Fisher (1993), Batschelet (1981), and Zar (1999); see Jenness (2012).
